chunks: And by this chain, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The testimony of the precursor of the pilgrims (the one who leads the group on wages) is not accepted because he kills his mount, consumes his provisions, exhausts himself, and takes his prayer lightly.
I said, 'And what about the hirer of camels, the camel-driver, and the navigator?' He said, 'And what is the problem with them? Their testimonies are accepted if they are righteous.'

key_terms.الْمُكَارِي: The hirer of camels (one who rents out camels)
key_terms.سَابِقِ الْحَاجِّ: Precursor/leader of the pilgrims (one who organizes and leads the group on wages)
key_terms.صُلَحَاءَ: Righteous/Good-tempered (plural of Ṣalīḥ, indicating moral integrity)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for accepting the testimony of Hajj group leaders and travel workers in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle that excessive worldly toil and neglect of religious duties (like prayer) can impair a witness's reliability, specifically disqualifying the 'Sābiq al-Ḥājj' who exhausts himself and his resources. Conversely, it validates the testimony of other travel workers provided they maintain 'Ṣulḥā’' (righteousness/integrity), highlighting that physical hardship alone does not invalidate testimony unless it leads to spiritual negligence. This ruling underscores the balance between professional duty and spiritual observance in establishing legal credibility.
